topicTitle: When the Search Result Is Wrong
skillLine: Tonight's Skill: Catch a fluent answer with the wrong source
missionLine: A customer missed their flight after Meridian's bot cited outdated visa guidance — now you're reviewing every retrieval-powered assistant before the next one goes out wrong.
incidentHeadline: The retrieval logs are full of confident answers built on the wrong document.
stakesLines: Every answer cites a real source
1 in 5 citations is the wrong version
Staff are acting on it before anyone checks
memoryLine: A real source is not the same as the right source.
reflectionPrompt: What would you check before trusting a cited answer?
escalationLine: Meridian's ops lead just messaged: "Two more customers just called in. Retrieval Confidence can't keep dropping like this."

cards.prompt: Review item #1 — the travel bot retrieves a 2023 visa page and tells a customer their passport needs no visa this summer. Clear it, or flag it?
cards.optionA: No visa is needed; the policy page clearly says so.
cards.optionB: Check the effective date and current official policy before relying on the retrieved page.
cards.explanation: Flag it. Retrieval found a real page, just not necessarily a current one — this is the exact pattern behind the missed-flight incident. A fluent answer can faithfully repeat stale evidence and still send someone to the airport with a surprise.

cards.prompt: Review item #2 — an employee asks about parental leave. The bot retrieves a contractor handbook and gives its rules as company policy. Clear it, or flag it?
cards.optionA: The handbook is close enough; both groups work for the same company.
cards.optionB: Verify the document's audience and policy scope before treating it as the employee's answer.
cards.explanation: Flag it. The wrong source can still be an official source. Retrieval needs a match on who the rule applies to, not just a keyword match on 'leave.'

cards.prompt: Review item #3 — a support bot cites a cached help article and tells a customer a feature is unavailable, though the release notes enabled it yesterday. Clear it, or flag it?
cards.optionA: Trust the cached article; it is part of the bot's approved knowledge base.
cards.optionB: Prefer the newer, authoritative release record and fix the stale retrieval source.
cards.explanation: Flag it. Approved does not mean current forever. The answer is polished because the source is polished; that doesn't stop it being yesterday's news.

cards.prompt: Review item #4 — a procurement bot retrieves a blog post quoting a supplier's old pricing, then gives the quote with a citation. Clear it, or flag it?
cards.optionA: Use the quote; the bot cited its source and the numbers are specific.
cards.optionB: Request the supplier's current price sheet; a citation shows where the claim came from, not that it is current or binding.
cards.explanation: Flag it. A source can be traceable and still be unsuitable for the decision. Citation is a clue to inspect, not a gold star for correctness.

cards.prompt: Review item #5 — a policy bot answers a UK tax question using a retrieved US IRS article because both mention 'self-employment expenses.' Clear it, or flag it?
cards.optionA: The rule is probably the same; the article covers the same kind of expense.
cards.optionB: Do not apply it; jurisdiction is part of the question, so the retrieved source is off-target.
cards.explanation: Flag it. Semantic search is good at finding similar words, not at noticing legal borders. The answer may be perfectly clear about the wrong country.

cards.prompt: Review item #6 — an engineering assistant retrieves an archived API reference and recommends a parameter removed in v4. Clear it, or flag it?
cards.optionA: Use the parameter; the archive is official documentation and includes an example.
cards.optionB: Use the version-matched reference; an official archive is still an archive.
cards.explanation: Flag it. The model did retrieve documentation, just documentation for a different reality. Version labels are evidence, not decorative metadata.

cards.prompt: Review item #7 — a health-plan assistant retrieves a summary page and says a treatment is covered, skipping the linked exclusions. Clear it, or flag it?
cards.optionA: It is covered; the summary says the plan includes that treatment.
cards.optionB: Check the governing plan terms and exclusions before giving a coverage answer.
cards.explanation: Flag it. A summary can be true and still incomplete for the case in front of you. Retrieval often grabs the friendly paragraph before the qualifying sentence hiding two clicks away.

cards.prompt: Review item #8 — the last one in tonight's queue: a campus bot retrieves two parking notices, one campus-wide and one for a single garage, and applies the garage closure to everyone. Clear it, or flag it?
cards.optionA: All parking is closed; the notice was retrieved for a parking question.
cards.optionB: Check the location and scope; a relevant document may still answer a narrower question than the user asked.
cards.explanation: Flag it. Search found a match on 'parking,' not necessarily on the whole situation. Good retrieval is not just finding a document; it's finding the document that governs this case.

checkpointCard.prompt: Final review before the incident report — a bot says a refund window is 30 days, citing a policy page last updated before the company changed it to 14. Clear it, or flag it?
checkpointCard.optionA: Honor 30 days because the bot produced a cited policy page.
checkpointCard.optionB: Verify the policy version and effective date; the citation may document a rule that no longer applies.
checkpointCard.explanation: Flag it. The problem was never that the bot made up a page — same as every item tonight. It trusted an outdated one, which can look almost exactly as convincing.

feynmanScript: In the visa, leave, and API items you just reviewed, the bot always had a source — just the wrong, old, or too-narrow one. Retrieval gives a model something to read; it doesn't guarantee the document governs the case in front of it. Check the date, audience, version, and scope before fluent becomes final.
